Story · Lesson 1

Adam's First Flying Lesson

After years of dreaming and saving, Adam finally sits in a cockpit. Read the story, then read it from his instructor's point of view.

Say what had been happening before a moment in the pastExplain a resultTell a story about a big day

1The story

For as long as he could remember, Adam had wanted to fly. By the time he was twenty, he had been reading about planes for ten years, he had been watching flight videos every night, and, for the last two years, he had been saving every pound he could. He had been working at his uncle's shop on weekends, and he had been taking fewer rickshaws and walking more.

Last Saturday, it finally happened. Adam arrived at the small flying school outside the city at seven in the morning. He was nervous. He had been lying awake since four, going over the instructions in his head. His instructor, Captain Nour, was waiting by a small white plane. "You look tired," she said. "Did you sleep?" "Not really," Adam admitted. "I had been dreaming about this day for so long that I couldn't close my eyes."

Captain Nour explained everything, the controls, the radio, and the checks they had to do before take-off. Then they climbed in. When the engine started, the whole plane shook. Adam held the controls with both hands. "Gently," said Captain Nour. "The plane wants to fly. Just let it."

They rolled down the runway, faster and faster, and then, suddenly, the ground fell away beneath them. Adam looked down. The Nile was shining in the morning sun, and the city looked like a map. He had been imagining this moment for half his life, but nothing had prepared him for how beautiful it was. When they landed thirty minutes later, his legs were shaking. Captain Nour smiled. "Not bad for a first flight. Same time next week?" Adam couldn't speak. He just nodded, grinning from ear to ear.

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
How long had Adam been reading about planes by the time he was twenty?For ten years.
2
What had he been doing for the last two years?Saving every pound he could.
3
Where had he been working on weekends?At his uncle's shop.
4
What time did he arrive at the flying school?At seven in the morning.
5
Why was Adam tired?He had been lying awake since four.
6
Who was his instructor?Captain Nour.
7
Why couldn't he sleep?He had been dreaming about this day for so long.
8
What happened when the engine started?The whole plane shook.
9
What did Captain Nour tell him?"Gently. The plane wants to fly. Just let it."
10
What did the Nile look like from above?It was shining in the morning sun.
11
How long was the flight?Thirty minutes.
12
How did Adam answer "Same time next week?"He nodded, grinning from ear to ear.

3Point of view Now Captain Nour tells it.

CN

Last Saturday, a young man called Adam came for his first lesson. I could see that he had wanted this for years. He told me that he had been saving for two years and had been working at his uncle's shop every weekend.

He looked tired. He had been lying awake since four o'clock, he said, because he had been dreaming about this day for so long. I have seen that look many times.

When the engine started, he held the controls so tightly that his hands went white. "Gently," I told him. "The plane wants to fly."

After take-off, he went completely quiet. He looked down at the Nile as if he had been waiting his whole life to see it from the sky. When we landed, his legs were shaking, but his smile was enormous. I think he will make a good pilot.

4What did you learn?

You learned the past perfect continuous.

We use it for an action that was continuing up to a moment in the past, often to explain a result or to say how long.

Continuing before that momentThe moment in the past
He had been saving for two yearswhen he finally booked his lesson.
He had been lying awake since four,so he was tired.
He had been dreaming about it for years,and at last it happened.
How long had he been waiting?Since he was a child.
had + been + -ingI had been waiting. They had been working.
Continuing or finished?He had been saving (continuing). He had saved 2,000 pounds (finished).
It often explains a resultHe was tired because he had been lying awake.
QuestionsWhat had you been doing before you started this course?I had been working in a shop.

5New words

admittedsaid that something was true, although it was not easy to say
instructora person who teaches a practical skill
controlsthe parts you use to drive or fly a machine
runwaythe long road where planes take off and land
beneathunder
grinningsmiling widely

Topic · Lesson 2

Managing Your Money

Budgets, needs and wants, saving, and debt. A few habits that make a big difference.

Talk about money and budgetsSeparate needs from wantsGive advice about saving

1Read

For many students, money is a constant worry. Prices keep rising, and it is easy to reach the end of the month with an empty wallet. The good news is that a few simple habits can make a big difference.

The first step is to make a budget, a simple plan of how much money comes in and how much goes out. Write down your income, from a part-time job, your family, or a scholarship. Then write down your expenses, such as transport, food, phone credit, and books. Many people are surprised when they see how much they spend on small things, like snacks and taxis.

Next, divide your expenses into needs and wants. Needs are things you can't live without, such as food, rent, and transport to work or university. Wants are nice but not necessary, like new shoes, a better phone, or eating out. Many experts suggest a simple rule. Spend about fifty percent of your income on needs and thirty percent on wants, and save the other twenty percent.

Saving is easier if you do it first. On the day you get paid, put some money aside before you spend anything. Even a small amount grows over time. Omar, who manages a phone shop, says, "I had been saving for six months before I noticed. Then one day, I had enough for a laptop."

Finally, be careful with debt. Borrowing money from friends or shops can feel easy, but paying it back can be hard. If you have to borrow, make a clear plan to repay it.

2The 50 / 30 / 20 rule

50%needs · food, rent, transport
30%wants · clothes, eating out
20%saving

3Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
What is a budget?A simple plan of how much money comes in and how much goes out.
2
What are expenses? Give two examples.The money you spend, for example on transport and food.
3
What is the difference between needs and wants?Needs are things you can't live without. Wants are nice but not necessary.
4
What does the 50 / 30 / 20 rule suggest?Spend 50% on needs and 30% on wants, and save 20%.
5
When is the best time to save?On the day you get paid, before you spend anything.
6
What should you do if you have to borrow money?Make a clear plan to repay it.

4New words

constanthappening all the time
walleta small case for money and cards
scholarshipmoney that is given to a student to pay for study
rentthe money you pay to live in a home
asideaway, to keep for later
repaypay back

There's a Problem With My Room

Making a polite complaint at a hotel

Make a polite complaintExplain what had been happeningChoose between solutions

1Read the conversation

Sara is staying at a hotel in Port Sudan for an engineering conference. She calls the reception desk.
CLCLERKGood evening, reception. How can I help you?
SSARAHello. I'm in room 214. I'm afraid there's a problem with my room.
CLCLERKI'm sorry to hear that. What seems to be the problem?
SSARAThe air conditioning isn't working. It had been making a strange noise all afternoon, and now it has stopped completely.
CLCLERKI apologize. Have you tried the remote control?
SSARAYes, I had been trying for twenty minutes before I called. And the room is very hot.
CLCLERKI understand. I can send someone to repair it, or I can move you to another room.
SSARAI'd prefer to move, please. I have an early meeting tomorrow, and I need to sleep.
CLCLERKOf course. Room 305 is ready. Someone will bring you the key in five minutes, and breakfast is free tomorrow, to say sorry.
SSARAThat's very kind. Thank you for your help.

2Useful phrases

Start politely

I'm afraid there's a problem with my room.

Describe the problem

The air conditioning isn't working.

Say what had been happening

It had been making a strange noise all afternoon.

Say what you tried

I had been trying for twenty minutes before I called.

Choose a solution

I'd prefer to move, please.

Accept an apology

That's very kind. Thank you for your help.

3New words

conferencea large meeting for people who do the same kind of work
receptionthe desk near the door of a hotel
air conditioninga machine that makes the air cool
apologizesay sorry
remote controla small device that controls a machine from a distance

Story · Lesson 4

If Omar Hadn't Missed the Bus

One bad morning, a chain of small events, and a new future. Read the story, then read it from the point of view of the man Omar helped.

Imagine a different pastUse the third conditionalTalk about regrets and luck

1The story

Last March, Omar woke up late. His phone battery had died in the night, so the alarm hadn't rung. He ran to the bus stop, but he was too late. The bus was already disappearing down the road. "Great," he thought. "Now I'll be late for my exam."

He decided to walk to the next stop. On the way, he passed an old man who was standing next to a car with its hood open. The man looked worried. Omar stopped. "Can I help?" The engine had stopped, and the man had no idea why. Omar looked inside, found a loose cable, and fixed it in two minutes. The man thanked him and offered him a ride to the university.

In the car, they talked. The man asked Omar about his studies and his work at the phone shop. Then he gave Omar his card. His name was Dr. Idris Mahmoud, and he was the director of a big technology company. "We're looking for young people who can solve problems," he said. "Call me after your exams."

Three months later, Omar started an internship at the company. Now, when he tells the story, he always laughs. "If my battery hadn't died, I wouldn't have missed the bus. If I hadn't missed the bus, I wouldn't have walked past that car. And if I hadn't stopped to help, I would never have met Dr. Idris." Adam always adds, "And if you had been on time, you would still be fixing phones!"

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Why didn't Omar's alarm ring?His phone battery had died in the night.
2
Did he catch the bus?No, he didn't. It was already disappearing down the road.
3
What did he decide to do?Walk to the next stop.
4
Who did he see on the way?An old man next to a car with its hood open.
5
What was wrong with the car?There was a loose cable.
6
How long did it take Omar to fix it?Two minutes.
7
What did the man offer him?A ride to the university.
8
Who was the man?Dr. Idris Mahmoud, the director of a big technology company.
9
What kind of people is his company looking for?Young people who can solve problems.
10
What happened three months later?Omar started an internship at the company.
11
What would have happened if Omar hadn't stopped to help?He would never have met Dr. Idris.
12
What does Adam always add?If Omar had been on time, he would still be fixing phones!

3Point of view Now Dr. Idris tells it.

DI

Last March, my car broke down on the way to the office. I was standing by the road, feeling helpless, when a young man stopped and asked if he could help. He found a loose cable and fixed it in two minutes.

I offered him a ride, and we talked. He had missed his bus that morning, he said. If he hadn't missed it, he wouldn't have been walking past my car.

I was impressed. He was polite, practical, and calm. So I gave him my card. Three months later, he joined our company as an intern, and he is one of the best we have ever had.

I often think about that morning. If my car hadn't broken down, I would never have found Omar. Sometimes the worst mornings bring the best people.

4What did you learn?

You learned the third conditional.

We use it to imagine a different past, what would have happened if something had been different.

If + had + past participlewould have + past participle
If my battery hadn't died,I wouldn't have missed the bus.
If I hadn't missed the bus,I wouldn't have walked past that car.
If I hadn't stopped to help,I would never have met Dr. Idris.
If his car hadn't broken down,he wouldn't have found Omar.
For a past that didn't happenIt's too late to change it. We only imagine it.
Short forms: I'd have · wouldn't haveI'd have = I would have.
Regrets: I wish I had…I wish I had set two alarms!
QuestionsWhat would you have done if you had missed the bus?I would have taken a rickshaw.

5New words

hoodthe metal cover over a car's engine
loosenot fixed firmly
ridea trip in someone's car
directorthe person who manages a company
internshipa period of work where you learn a job
impressedthinking that someone is very good at something

I'm So Sorry

Apologizing to a customer and putting a mistake right

Apologize properlyExplain what went wrongOffer a solution

1Read the conversation

A customer has come back to Omar's phone shop. Her phone was repaired yesterday, but now her photos are gone.
CCUSTOMERExcuse me. I picked up my phone yesterday, but all my photos are gone!
OOMAROh no. I'm so sorry. Let me look at it.
CCUSTOMERThose were photos of my daughter's wedding. They're very important to me.
OOMARI completely understand. I think my colleague reset the phone by mistake. If he had checked first, this wouldn't have happened.
CCUSTOMERSo are they lost forever?
OOMARNot necessarily. Did you have a backup, maybe online?
CCUSTOMERI don't know. My son set up the phone for me.
OOMARLet me check. Yes! Your photos were saved to your online account. I can bring them all back now.
CCUSTOMEROh, thank goodness! If you hadn't found them, I would have cried all week.
OOMARAgain, I apologize. There's no charge for the repair, and we'll be more careful in the future.

2Useful phrases

Apologize

I'm so sorry.

Show you understand

I completely understand.

Explain the mistake

My colleague reset the phone by mistake.

Say what should have happened

If he had checked first, this wouldn't have happened.

Offer a solution

There's no charge for the repair.

Promise

We'll be more careful in the future.

3New words

colleaguea person you work with
resetreturn a machine to how it was when it was new
by mistakenot on purpose
necessarilyin every case
backupa copy you keep in case the first one is lost
chargethe price you pay for a service

Story · Lesson 6

The Letter in the Old Book

Huda finds a letter from 1975 inside a library book. Who wrote it, and why was it never sent? Read the story, then read it from the writer's point of view.

Guess what happened in the pastUse must have and can't haveExplain how sure you are

1The story

Huda works part-time at the university library. One quiet afternoon, she was putting old books back on the shelves when an envelope fell out of a book about planes. The paper was yellow, and the stamp showed a picture of the Nile. The date on the letter was March 12, 1975.

"Dear Amna," it began. "Tomorrow I leave for Cairo to study engineering. I wanted to say this to you in person, but I couldn't find the courage. Will you wait for me?" It was signed only with the letter Y.

Huda read it again and again. "He must have been very young," she thought. "And he must have loved her very much." But the letter had never been posted. "Amna can't have read it, or it wouldn't still be here. He might have forgotten it in the book. Or he might have changed his mind."

That evening, she showed the letter to Adam and Sara at the café. Adam went quiet. He looked at the handwriting for a long time. "This must be a mistake," he said slowly. "My grandfather's name is Yousif. He studied engineering in Cairo. And my grandmother's name is Amna."

The next day, Adam took the letter to his grandparents' house. His grandfather put on his glasses and read it. Then he laughed until he had tears in his eyes. "I wrote this the night before I left! I must have left it in the library book. I looked for it everywhere." His grandmother smiled. "So that's why you never asked me. For four years, I thought you must have forgotten me."

"But in the end, you waited," said Adam. "Yes," said his grandmother, holding the letter. "Fifty years late, but I finally got it."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
Where does Huda work?At the university library.
2
What fell out of the book?An envelope.
3
What was the book about?Planes.
4
What was the date on the letter?March 12, 1975.
5
Where was the writer going to study?In Cairo.
6
How was the letter signed?Only with the letter Y.
7
Why did Huda think Amna can't have read it?Because it was still in the book. It had never been posted.
8
Who did Huda show the letter to?Adam and Sara.
9
What is the name of Adam's grandfather?Yousif.
10
What did his grandfather do when he read the letter?He laughed until he had tears in his eyes.
11
What had his grandmother thought for four years?That he must have forgotten her.
12
How late did she get the letter?Fifty years late.

3Point of view Now Adam's grandfather tells it.

G

In March 1975, the night before I left for Cairo, I wrote a letter to Amna, the girl I loved. I was too shy to speak to her, so I put everything on paper.

The next morning, I couldn't find it anywhere. I must have left it in the library book I had been reading. I thought that she must have read it and said no, because she never wrote to me.

For four years, I was afraid to ask her. When I came back, I finally found the courage. She said yes, and we have been married for forty-six years.

Last week, my grandson came to the house with that same letter. A young woman at the library had found it. I laughed and cried at the same time. Amna can't have known how I felt in 1975. Now, at last, she does.

4What did you learn?

You learned modals for the past.

We use them to guess about the past from what we know now, and to show how sure we are.

How sure?Example
Almost 100% yes: must haveHe must have loved her very much.
Maybe: might have · could haveHe might have forgotten it in the book.
Almost 100% no: can't have · couldn't haveAmna can't have read it.
Now, not the past: must beThis must be a mistake.
modal + have + past participlemust have left, might have changed, can't have known
Not mustn't haveFor no, say can't have. Not mustn't have.
Say it fastmust have sounds like "must-uv" when we speak fast.
QuestionsYour friend didn't come to class yesterday. Why not?He might have been sick.

5New words

shelvesflat boards on a wall for books
envelopea paper cover for a letter
stampa small paper you put on a letter to pay for posting it
couragethe ability to do something that frightens you
handwritingthe way a person writes with a pen
marriedbeing husband and wife

Science · Lesson 7

What Happened to the Dinosaurs?

The clues that tell scientists what must have happened sixty-six million years ago.

Explain scientific evidenceGuess about the past with must have and might haveDescribe a chain of events

1Read

For more than 150 million years, dinosaurs ruled the Earth. Then, about sixty-six million years ago, they disappeared, together with about three quarters of all life on the planet. For a long time, nobody knew why. Today, most scientists agree on the answer, and it came from space.

The first clue was found in 1980. A father and son, Luis and Walter Alvarez, were studying rocks in Italy. In a thin layer of clay from exactly that time, they found a lot of iridium, a metal that is rare on Earth but common in rocks from space. They had an idea. A huge rock from space, an asteroid, must have hit the Earth.

But if an asteroid had hit the Earth, it must have left a giant hole, a crater. Where was it? Ten years later, scientists found it under the sea and land near Chicxulub, in Mexico. It is about 180 kilometers wide. The asteroid that made it must have been about ten kilometers across, as big as a city.

The impact must have been terrible. It caused fires, huge waves, and enormous clouds of dust. The dust blocked the sun for months, maybe years. Without sunlight, plants died, then the animals that ate plants, and then the animals that ate them.

Some scientists think that giant volcanoes in India might have made things worse at the same time. But not everything died. Small animals survived, and so did some dinosaurs. The birds outside your window are their great-great-grandchildren.

2A chain of events

1Impacta 10 km asteroid hits Mexico
2Dustclouds block the sun
3Coldplants stop growing
4Hungerbig animals die out
Did you know?

Birds are living dinosaurs. A chicken is closer to Tyrannosaurus rex than a crocodile is.

3Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
How long did dinosaurs rule the Earth?For more than 150 million years.
2
When did they disappear?About sixty-six million years ago.
3
What did Luis and Walter Alvarez find in 1980?A lot of iridium in a thin layer of clay.
4
Why was the iridium an important clue?It is rare on Earth but common in rocks from space.
5
Where is the crater?Near Chicxulub, in Mexico.
6
How big must the asteroid have been?About ten kilometers across, as big as a city.
7
Why did plants die?The dust blocked the sun for months, maybe years.
8
Which living animals are related to dinosaurs?Birds.

4New words

ruledcontrolled or were the most powerful
layerone level of something that lies over another
rarenot found very often
impactthe moment when one thing hits another
volcanoesmountains that send out fire and hot rock
survivedstayed alive after something dangerous

Where's My Package?

Calling a delivery company about a lost package

Explain a problem on the phoneGuess what might have happenedAsk for a clear next step

1Read the conversation

Sara ordered a new laptop online. The website says it was delivered yesterday, but she never received it. She calls the delivery company.
AGAGENTGood morning, Speed Delivery. How can I help?
SSARAHello. I'm calling about a package. The website says it was delivered yesterday, but I never got it. The tracking number is SD 4 5 1 2 9.
AGAGENTI'm sorry about that. Let me check. It says the driver left it at 3:15 yesterday afternoon. Were you at home?
SSARANo, I was at the university. Could he have left it with a neighbor?
AGAGENTHe might have. Or it might have gone to the wrong address. Let me check the photo. Is your door green?
SSARANo, it's white! He must have delivered it to the wrong house.
AGAGENTI see. I'll contact the driver now and ask him to collect it. Can we deliver it again tomorrow morning?
SSARAYes, please. And can he call me before he comes?
AGAGENTOf course. You'll get a call before ten. I apologize again for the trouble.

2Useful phrases

Explain the problem

The website says it was delivered, but I never got it.

Give information

The tracking number is SD 4 5 1 2 9.

Guess politely

Could he have left it with a neighbor?

Be sure

He must have delivered it to the wrong house.

Ask for the next step

Can we deliver it again tomorrow morning?

Make a request

Can he call me before he comes?

3New words

packagesomething that is wrapped and sent by post
deliveredtaken to a person or place
tracking numbera number that shows where a package is
neighbora person who lives next to you
collectgo and get something
troubleproblems or worry

Story · Lesson 9

Letters to Our Future Selves

Mr. Ali asks his students to write to the people they will be in ten years. Read the story, then read it from Mr. Ali's point of view.

Talk about the future in progressSay what will be finished by a timeWrite about your plans and dreams

1The story

On the last day of the course, Mr. Ali came into the classroom with a box. "Today," he said, "you are going to write a letter. Not to me, and not to your family. You're going to write to yourself, the person you will be in ten years." He explained that he would keep the letters in the box and post them to the students in exactly ten years.

Everyone laughed, but then the room went quiet. Ten years felt like a very long time.

Adam wrote first. "Dear Adam, by the time you read this, you will have finished your training, and you will have flown hundreds of hours. I hope you will be flying big planes between Khartoum and the rest of the world. Please don't forget the first time you saw the Nile from the sky."

Sara wrote about water. "In ten years, I will be working as an engineer, I hope in Kassala or Darfur. By then, our team will have built pumps in fifty villages. And I will still be arguing with Adam about everything."

Omar's letter was short. "Dear Omar, I don't know where you will be living, but I know you will have started your own company. Don't forget who helped you, and always stop for people by the road."

Huda wrote slowly and carefully. "Dear Huda, by now you will have been a teacher for eight years. You will be standing in front of a class, just like Mr. Ali. I hope your students will be as lucky as you were."

When they had finished, Mr. Ali collected the letters and closed the box. "In ten years," he said, smiling, "I will be sitting at home, drinking tea and waiting for the postman to bring me your answers."

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

1
What did Mr. Ali bring into the classroom?A box.
2
Who were the students going to write to?To themselves, the person they will be in ten years.
3
When will the students get their letters?In exactly ten years.
4
What did the room do after everyone laughed?It went quiet.
5
What will Adam have finished by the time he reads the letter?His training.
6
Where does Adam hope he will be flying?Between Khartoum and the rest of the world.
7
Where does Sara hope she will be working?In Kassala or Darfur.
8
How many villages will her team have built pumps in?Fifty.
9
What will Omar have started?His own company.
10
What advice does Omar give himself?Always stop for people by the road.
11
How long will Huda have been a teacher?For eight years.
12
What will Mr. Ali be doing in ten years?Sitting at home, drinking tea and waiting for the postman.

3Point of view Now Mr. Ali tells it.

MA

Every year, on the last day of the course, I ask my students to write a letter to themselves. I keep the letters in a box and post them ten years later.

This year, Adam wrote that he will have finished his pilot training and will be flying big planes. Sara believes her team will have built pumps in fifty villages, and I believe her.

Omar is sure he will have started his own company. Huda wrote that she will be standing in front of a class, like me. That made me very proud.

In ten years, I will have been a teacher for forty years. I will be sitting at home with my tea, and I will be waiting for the postman, because every year, some of my students write back.

4What did you learn?

You learned the future continuous and the future perfect.

We use the future continuous for an action in progress at a time in the future, and the future perfect for an action that will be finished before that time.

In progress then: will be + -ingFinished before then: will have + past participle
I will be flying big planes.I will have finished my training.
I will be working as an engineer.Our team will have built fifty pumps.
Where will you be living?Will you have started a company?
This time next year, I will be studying.By next year, I will have passed my exams.
With byBy 2035, by then, by the time you read this, use the future perfect.
How long: will have beenBy now, you will have been a teacher for eight years.
Short forms: I'll be · I'll haveI'll be working. I'll have finished.
QuestionsWhat will you be doing this time next year?I'll be studying at university.

5New words

future selvesthe people we will be later in life
traininglearning the skills for a job
arguingspeaking angrily with someone because you don't agree
carefullywith a lot of attention
proudhappy because of what someone has done
postmana person who brings letters to your home

Podcast · Lesson 10

The Future of Work

Sara and Adam ask an expert what work will look like in ten years, and how students can get ready.

Follow a podcastTalk about the future of jobsUse will be doing and will have done

1Before you listen

What jobs do you think computers will do in ten years?

What do you think you will be doing in ten years?

2Listen and read The Future Vision Podcast · Episode 12

Hosts: Sara and Adam · Guest: Dr. Amira Salih, who studies technology and jobs
00:05SSARAWelcome to The Future Vision Podcast! I'm Sara.
00:08AADAMAnd I'm Adam. Today we're talking about the future of work. Our guest is Dr. Amira Salih, who studies technology and jobs. Welcome!
00:20DADR. AMIRAThank you. It's great to be here.
00:23SSARALet's start with a big question. What will work look like in ten years?
00:30DADR. AMIRAWell, by 2035, computers will have taken over many simple tasks, like typing and checking numbers. But people will still be doing the jobs that need creativity and care.
00:46AADAMSuch as?
00:48DADR. AMIRATeachers, nurses, engineers, designers. In ten years, a teacher won't be grading homework by hand. Software will be doing that. But she will still be explaining, listening, and encouraging her students.
01:09SSARASo what should students be doing now to prepare?
01:13DADR. AMIRAThree things. First, learn to use technology, don't fear it. Second, keep learning. By the time you're thirty, you'll probably have changed jobs two or three times. And third, practice working in teams. Machines are fast, but they aren't good with people.
01:38AADAMI'm training to be a pilot. Will planes be flying themselves?
01:43DADR. AMIRASome small ones already do! But passengers will be expecting a human in the cockpit for many years. I think your job is safe, Adam.
01:56AADAMThat's good news. My grandfather will be happy.
01:59SSARADr. Amira, one last question. What will you be doing in ten years?
02:04DADR. AMIRAProbably talking on podcasts about the next ten years!
02:09SSARAThank you so much. That's all for today. Next week, we'll be talking about money and young people. See you then!

Conversation · Lesson 11

The Job Interview

Answering the classic questions in a job interview

Introduce yourself in an interviewTalk about your strengths and weaknessesDescribe your plans for the future

1Read the conversation

Huda has an interview for a job as a teaching assistant at a primary school. Mrs. Karim, the head teacher, is interviewing her.
MKMRS. KARIMGood morning, Huda. Please have a seat. Can you tell me a little about yourself?
HHUDAOf course. I'm in my final year of a degree in education, and I've been helping at an English course for two years.
MKMRS. KARIMWhy do you want to work with children?
HHUDAI love seeing the moment when a child finally understands something. It's the best feeling in the world.
MKMRS. KARIMWhat would you say are your strengths and weaknesses?
HHUDAI'm patient, and I'm good at explaining things in different ways. If one way doesn't work, I try another. My weakness is that I sometimes spend too long preparing, but I'm learning to plan my time better.
MKMRS. KARIMWhere do you see yourself in five years?
HHUDAIn five years, I'll have finished my teacher training, and I'll be teaching my own class, I hope here. Could I ask what a typical day looks like for a teaching assistant?
MKMRS. KARIMGood question. You'll be working with small groups in the morning and helping in the library after lunch. Thank you, Huda. We'll let you know by Thursday.
HHUDAThank you for your time. I look forward to hearing from you.

2Useful phrases

Talk about yourself

I'm in my final year of a degree in education.

Say why you want the job

I love seeing the moment when a child finally understands.

Give a strength with an example

I'm patient. If one way doesn't work, I try another.

Turn a weakness into progress

I'm learning to plan my time better.

Talk about the future

In five years, I'll have finished my teacher training.

Ask a question and end politely

Could I ask what a typical day looks like?
I look forward to hearing from you.

3New words

interviewa meeting where someone asks you questions to decide if you can do a job
assistanta person who helps someone in their work
degreewhat you get when you finish university
strengthsthings you are good at
weaknessesthings you are not good at
typicalusual, normal

Story · Lesson 12

Lights Over the Nile

Strange lights appear over the river at night, and everyone has a theory. Read the story, then read it from the point of view of the person who knows the truth.

Report what people say and believeUse it is said that and is believed toTell a mystery story

1The story

It started on a Thursday in October. At about ten at night, people on the bridge in Khartoum saw three small lights moving slowly over the Nile. They went up, stopped, turned, and then disappeared behind the trees on the island.

By the next morning, everyone was talking about them. A video of the lights had been shared thousands of times. On the radio, a man said, "It is said that the lights have been seen before, many years ago." A woman at the market told Sara that they were believed to be the spirits of fishermen. A taxi driver was sure they were a secret plane from another country.

The newspapers loved the story. "MYSTERY LIGHTS OVER THE NILE," one headline said. "The lights are thought to be some kind of aircraft," the article explained, "but their origin is not known." Another paper wrote that the lights were reported to have appeared over the river every night that week.

Adam was fascinated. "Planes don't stop in the air," he said. "Whatever it is, it isn't a plane." Sara was more practical. "Let's go and look," she said.

So on Sunday night, the friends waited on the bridge. At ten o'clock exactly, the lights rose from the island. Sara looked through her binoculars, and then she began to laugh. "I know those lights," she said. "And I know whose they are."

On the island, standing behind the trees with a controller in his hands, was Omar. He and the engineers at his company had been testing a new delivery drone at night, when the sky was quiet. When the friends found him, he looked embarrassed. "I've seen the videos," he admitted. "Apparently, I'm a ghost, a spy, and a fisherman."

The next day, the company explained everything on the radio. But the story didn't completely die. Even now, it is said that on some nights, if you stand on the bridge at ten, you can still see the lights.

2Questions and answers Answer fast. Short answers are fine.

3

4

5

6
What was the taxi driver sure of?That they were a secret plane from another country.
7

8

9
What did Sara use to look at the lights?Binoculars.
10
Who was on the island?Omar.
11
What had he been testing?A new delivery drone.
12
What is still said about the bridge?That on some nights at ten, you can still see the lights.

3Point of view Now Omar tells it.

O

Our company is building a drone that can deliver medicine to villages. We decided to test it at night over the island, because the sky is quiet and nobody would see us. That was the plan, anyway.

The next morning, my phone was full of videos of my drone. It was said to be a secret plane. It was believed to be the spirits of fishermen. One newspaper wrote that the lights were thought to be some kind of aircraft. Well, that part was true.

On Sunday night, while I was flying it, I heard a laugh behind the trees. It was Sara, of course, with Adam and Huda. I have never been so embarrassed in my life.

We explained everything on the radio, but nobody wants a mystery to end. These days, it is said that the lights still appear. I'm not saying anything. But I sometimes test the drone on Thursdays.

4What did you learn?

You learned the passive with reporting verbs.

We use it to report what many people say, think, or believe, when we don't know who said it first or when it isn't important.

It + passive + that…Subject + passive + to…
It is said that the lights are spirits.The lights are said to be spirits.
It is believed that they are a secret plane.They are believed to be a secret plane.
It is thought that it is an aircraft.It is thought to be an aircraft.
It was reported that they appeared every night.They were reported to have appeared every night.
Common verbs: say · think · believe · report · expect · knowIt is expected that prices will rise.
About the past: to have + past participleHe is said to have built the bridge.
Often in news and formal EnglishLook for it in the newspaper and on the radio.
QuestionsWhat is said about your city or village?It is said that the old house is haunted.

5New words

spiritsthe part of a person that some believe lives on after death
aircrafta plane or another machine that flies
originwhere something comes from
fascinatedvery interested
binocularsan instrument for seeing things far away
embarrassedfeeling shy and uncomfortable because of something you did

News · Lesson 13

Students Build Solar Pump for Village

Read a real-style news article, and find the five key facts of the story.

Read a news articleFind who, what, where, when, and whyUnderstand: It is said that… / is expected to…

1Read the article

The Daily NileThursday, May 7

Students Build Solar Pump That Brings Water to a Village

A team of young engineers has given a village near Kassala clean water every day, using only the power of the sun.

By our science reporter

A village near Kassala has had clean water every day this month, thanks to a solar-powered water pump that was designed and built by a team of five engineering students. The pump is believed to be the first of its kind in the area.

Before the pump was installed, women and children in the village had been walking up to two hours a day to bring water from a well. "It used to take my whole morning," said one mother. "Now my children go to school on time."

“Now my children go to school on time.”A mother in the village

The pump is powered by six solar panels, and it is said to bring up more than ten thousand liters of water a day from deep under the ground. The water is stored in a large tank and cleaned before it is used. It is reported that the whole system cost less than a small car.

The team was led by Sara Osman, a second-year student. "We had been studying solar energy in class," she said, "but we wanted to see it change real lives." The students are expected to build two more pumps in nearby villages next year, and other universities are said to be interested in the design.

Engineers have welcomed the project. It is widely agreed that small, cheap solar systems could bring clean water to thousands of villages across Sudan.

2The five key facts

Who?five engineering students, led by Sara Osman
What?a solar-powered water pump
Where?a village near Kassala
When?this month
Why?the village had no clean water nearby
